hook: Excerpts from three Skylab mission technical debriefings (1973–1974) in which astronaut crews describe unusual visual phenomena: retinal light flashes possibly linked to cosmic rays, an unidentified bright reddish satellite in near-identical orbit to Skylab, and external flashing lights with relative motion.
why_it_matters: These are firsthand accounts from NASA astronauts describing unidentified objects in low Earth orbit that were never officially explained to the crews. The Skylab 3 observation is particularly notable: a bright reddish object held a near-identical orbit for 10 minutes, exhibited a measurable 10-second rotation period, and allowed the crew to estimate its range at 30–50 nautical miles — yet they explicitly stated no identification was ever provided. The document shows NASA crews were observing and formally reporting anomalous orbital objects and requesting answers through official debriefing channels.

key_findings.finding: Skylab 2 Science Pilot Joseph Kerwin reported light flashes seen with eyes closed, occurring at up to two or three per minute, appearing as spots, sunbursts, or streaks — primarily in peripheral vision. The crew discussed whether these correlated with the South Atlantic Anomaly and whether some were cosmic particle interactions.

quotes.text: We saw light flashes. I think all of us saw them. I saw them most often when I was in the sack at night with my eyes closed but awake naturally. They tended to wax and wane in frequency.

They were numerous at times - two or three per minute. Some of them to me were a spot or sunbursts. Some were streaks. The streaks, in my case, were less frequent than the bursts. Most of them were in my peripheral visual field.
I had a couple that I thought were cosmic particles. I saw an entrance streak and an exit streak.

key_findings.finding: The Skylab 2 crew explicitly affirmed the light flashes were not hallucinations, distinguishing them from a known fire sensor indicator aboard the station.

quotes.text: And you'd have to be careful that you weren't confusing that with the fire flash. Once you've seen a few of each, there is question of which is which. They're not an hallucination.

key_findings.finding: The Skylab 3 crew observed a bright reddish object in a near-identical orbit to Skylab for approximately 10 minutes, exhibiting a measurable 10-second brightness variation consistent with rotation. From the 5–7 second delay in its entry into darkness relative to Skylab, the crew estimated it was no more than 30–50 nautical miles away. It was never seen again and its identity was never explained to the crew.

quotes.text: This bright reddish object was out there and we tracked it for about 5 or 10 minutes. It was obviously a satellite in a very Similar orbit to our own. It was rotating and had a period of almost exactly 10 seconds because you could see the brightness vary with that period. We followed it until sunset and it went out of sunlight just about 5 to 7 seconds after we did.

From the 5- to 10-second delay in it's disappearance we surmised that it was not more than 30 to 50 nautical miles from our location. From it's original position in the wardroom window, it did not move more than 10 or 20 degrees over the 10 minutes or so that we watched it. It's orbit was very close to that of our own. We never saw it on any - earlier or succeeding orbits and we'd be quite interested in having its identification established.

key_findings.finding: The Skylab 3 crew attempted to image the reddish object using onboard monitors but could not resolve it beyond a bright light, and noted it was significantly brighter than any star or planet including Jupiter.

quotes.text: You might point out that it never did take the shape of an object but it was always brighter than any other star or planet in the night sky. It was much brighter.
We tried monitors and everything on it but we could never make it into anything other than a bright light.

key_findings.finding: Skylab 4 Commander Gerald Carr reported multiple sightings of external lights with definite motion relative to the station, some appearing to tumble, which the crew reported via dump tapes as soon as they occurred. They presumed — but did not confirm — these were Skylab debris or other satellites.

quotes.text: One other area of unusual events that we reported on the dump tapes was that on occasion we saw some lights flashing outside with very a definite motion relative to ours. We presumed that they were other pieces of Skylab, or possibly other satellites.
The fact that one or two of them appeared to be tumbling was apparently due to the oscillation of the light flashes that we were getting from them.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The Skylab 3 unidentified orbital object observation (1973) occurred after Project Blue Book's closure in 1969, representing the gap in formal UAP investigation where astronaut reports of anomalous objects had no established military reporting channel.

This document was included in the PURSUE release on war.gov, making it part of the corpus AARO is responsible for reviewing; the Skylab 3 reddish satellite observation is precisely the type of credentialed, instrumented orbital UAP report AARO now investigates.
